full_judgment: The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent on the other hand submits that there is no hard and fast rule for defining 'sufficient cause'. It will depend on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. In the instant case, the impugned order of dismissal of the appeal was made on 8.5.88 for want of steps by the appellants and their lawyer which they came to know about on the very day of dismissal of the appeal, but the Miscellaneous Case for restoration of the appeal after setting aside the impugned order of dismissal was filed only on5.6.88, of course within time, but after about 27 days. This shows the longness of the party to seek the relief under Order 41 rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure. However, when it is the case of the appellants that on the date fixed for hearing of the appeal i.e. 8.5.8'8 there was a duly engaged lawyer for them who claims to have been present in court with an application and the appellant No. 1 also claims to have come to the court at about 11:30 AM and on query came to learn about the facts of dismissal of the appeal, it is not understood what prevented the party that means the appellants or their duly appointed lawyer Mr. Shafiuddin to file immediately an application for restoration of the appeal after setting aside or recalling the impugned order of dismissal in the facts and circumstances as narrated in the Miscellaneous Case. It appears that the plea of filing an application on behalf of the appellants for time on 8.5.88 is bogus, when even the hazira on behalf of the appellants was not filed in court. This is undoubtedly a contumacious negligence and wilful default on behalf of the appellants as a well as on behalf of their duly engaged lawyer. In the case cited before me by Mr. Karmaker in AIR 1981 Punjab page 228 it appears that in that case an application for restoration was made within half an hour of the passing of the order of dismissal and apart from that, both the parties were absent on the date fixed for hearing, but in the instant case, the respondent was present and the appellant was absent with his lawyer and the application for restoration of the appeal on setting aside the impugned order of dismissal was filed after about 27 days. This exposes the negligent conduct of the party that means of the appellants as well as their learned lawyers. Thus it appears from the facts and circumstances of this case that the appellants as well as their engaged lawyers were guilty of contumacious negligence and as such they are not entitled to the benefit of construing their alleged negligence as sufficient cause and the aforesaid decision therefore does not help the appellants. The next point urged before me by Mr. Karmakar is that when the appellants or their lawyer were not found on call at 11:30 AM on 8.5.88, the court ought to have waited till the end of the day before passing the order of dismissal for default and that having not been done, the learned Additional District Judge committed error of law in passing the impugned order of dismissal and he has further committed illegality in taking into consideration the previous adjournments in the appeal. In support of his contentions, he has relied on a decision in the case of Badri Prasad and another Vs. Ambika Pershad and another, reported in AIR 1941, Oudh, 91. In the above case, an application was filed by the auction-purchaser for getting possession of the auction purchased land, but that application was dismissed for default at about 10/11 AM for the absence of the applicant-auction purchaser who of course rushed to the court within 15 minutes of the dismissal of the application and then and there filed petition for restoration of the said application in the forenoon of the same day and thereafter he went into the witness-box and stated on oath the facts and circumstances by which he was prevented from appearing in court when the application was taken up for hearing and made a prayer for setting aside the order of dismissal for default, and restoration of the application for hearing Mr. Karmakar has also relied on a decision in the case of Rayapprolu Viswandham Vs.
